account: Compiled a stock of 6 concrete illustration items for the AI-art-and-kitsch essay, balanced present (AI 'slop' on social feeds, the AI default look) and past (sentimental greeting-card/calendar kitsch, formulaic salon painting, photography-accused-of-degrading-art, recorded/mechanical music debates). Each item has a one-line claim plus a plain 2-3 sentence description, with explicit uncertainty flags as the acceptance condition requires. Because the dossier supplies no source materials (stated in separator_facts and the brief itself), every claim rests on the writer's general knowledge and is flagged as uncertain; no invented statistics, quotations, exhibitions, or proper names were introduced, and the two historical names alluded to (Baudelaire, Sousa) are caveated rather than pinned to exact words.
assumptions: The writer is expected to observe current AI-image phenomena directly (c1, c2) and to rely on remembered general history for the past items (c3-c6).

The acceptance condition's ban on invented statistics, quotations, exhibitions, and proper names is interpreted as overriding concreteness: names and any quotation-like phrasing are kept generic or heavily caveated.

boundary_findings.alternative_explanation: The parent may intend the historical items to remain genre-level and anonymous, in which case concreteness must come solely from the observable present-day items (c1, c2).
boundary_findings.consequence_if_absorbed: If the parent treats remembered attributions as verified fact, the essay may ship a false quotation or misattribution, directly violating the acceptance condition and undercutting the essay's persuasive credibility.
boundary_findings.narrative: The acceptance condition forbids inventing statistics, quotations, exhibitions, or proper names, while the node objective simultaneously demands 'vivid, truthful particulars' and the historical items necessarily rest on remembered names/attributions (Baudelaire, Sousa, salon practice) that this no-source dossier cannot verify. The concrete-vs-no-invention tension is real and unresolved.
boundary_findings.smallest_suspected_scope: the historical examples c4-c6 and any specific-name claims

boundary_findings.alternative_explanation: The parent may deliberately keep examples thesis-neutral, selecting positions later.
boundary_findings.consequence_if_absorbed: If this node were to drift into essay prose or pre-commit a thesis, it would violate the brief's 'raw material only' instruction and could pre-slant examples against decision:2's neutrality requirement.
boundary_findings.narrative: The node's demands (D2, D3) concern genre and thesis, whereas this child node's objective is to supply raw example material; the essay prose is forbidden here ('this brief is raw material only, not essay prose'). There is a boundary between example-stock and thesis-argument that is not specified further upstream.
boundary_findings.smallest_suspected_scope: the handoff from this brief to the essay draft

citations.excerpt: essay on AI art and kitsch

counterevidence: Prevalence figures for this content are not reliable from general knowledge; do not cite any statistic.
A share of such images is nearly indistinguishable from mass-produced stock photography, so 'instantly recognizable' is true for a large but not a universal share.
claims.statement: Social-media feeds now carry a widespread flood of glossy, symmetrical, sentimental AI images - grandmothers, perfect babies, wolves, nativity scenes - that many regular users instantly recognize as machine-made 'slop.'

counterevidence: The look shifts quickly as model versions improve, so a static description risks dating easily.
Newer generators increasingly avoid gross anatomy errors, making such slips less universal than in 2022-2023.
claims.statement: AI image generators have produced a trademark default look: waxy, airbrushed skin, glassy symmetrical faces, soft diffuse light, heavy gloss and saturation, and recurrent anatomy slips such as extra or misjointed fingers and garbled text.

counterevidence: No specific artist or publisher is named to avoid any invented attribution; this is a genre-level characterization.
The 'big-eyed waifs' subgenre is real but best described generically rather than tied to a particular maker.
claims.statement: Sentimental human-made kitsch - glossy greeting-card puppies and cottages, idealizing calendar landscapes, tearful waif portraits - occupied the same emotional niche long before AI.

counterevidence: This is a general historical characterization of 19th-century salon practice, not an account of a specific exhibition; avoid naming any show or painter.
The word 'mechanical' was applied to such painting by critics, but pinning the exact usage to a source is beyond general knowledge.
claims.statement: A century and a half ago, formulaic academic/salon painting was already suspected of being mechanical because it worked from a stock kit of classical mythologies, idealized nudes, and smoothly 'finished' surfaces.

counterevidence: Attribution to Charles Baudelaire's 1859 salon review is a remembered association and is flagged as moderately uncertain; do not quote exact words.
The exact strength and wording of the accusation varied by critic, so describe it generally.
claims.statement: When photography arrived in the mid-1800s, prominent critics charged that it would degrade art by pandering to a mass public and by copying appearances instead of exercising imagination.

counterevidence: The association with John Philip Sousa's essay 'The Menace of Mechanical Music' (c. 1906) is recalled but flagged as moderately uncertain; do not quote it.
Fears of standardized sound also blended with broader anxieties about mass reproduction, so scope the claim to the general worry.
claims.statement: Early recorded and mechanical music was likewise feared as a standardized substitute that would crowd out living, improvised performance.

counterevidence: The dossier contains no source materials whatsoever (see separator_facts: 'No source materials are provided'); every claim here derives from the writer's general knowledge and should be treated by the parent as unverified memory, not established fact.

No statistics about AI slop prevalence, and no verifiable dates, venues, or attributions for the historical debates, are available in the packet; anything numeric or precisely attributed must be dropped or hedged.
next_observation: Seek any general reference, if one appears, to verify the Baudelaire 1859 and Sousa 1906 attributions before the parent leans on them; absent that, keep both purely generic and hedged.
unresolved: Primary verification for the two historical associations - Baudelaire's 1859 salon remarks and Sousa's 'Menace of Mechanical Music' - remains outstanding; the parent should treat them as indicative color, not load-bearing facts.
Whether the essay wants exactly four, five, or six items is unspecified; this stock supplies six, any of which can be dropped.
